scenes.text: There are billions of hours of screen recordings that show people how to use software. Tutorials, walkthroughs, training videos. AI agents can't learn from any of it.

Today, agents learn tasks from text: prompts, documents, hand-written skills. Recent research lets agents glance at tutorial videos as hints, and it helps by only a few points. And when an agent goes off track, it usually doesn't know.
Eye-doss turns a video into a program. It learns the form of a task, not the pixels. And every step carries a visual contract, so the agent can check that it did what the person did.

Here's a fourteen second tutorial, recorded with a highlighted pointer. A totals row gets added to a spreadsheet. From the video frames alone, Eye-doss finds every click and drag, reads what was typed, and records what each step changed on screen.
Then it works out what each step was for. E2 to E11 isn't an address to copy. It's the Revenue column, over all the data rows. And the bold button is understood by its effect: the text got heavier.

Now run the skill where the video never went. The app has been redesigned: dark theme, new layout, columns shuffled. Copying the clicks falls apart. Eye-doss finds the Revenue column where it moved, rewrites the formula, and checks every step before it moves on.
Even a completely different spreadsheet app. Same skill, rewritten for the new screen, and checked.

And when something gets in the way, like a dialog that pops up halfway through, the contracts are what save the run. Eye-doss notices the step didn't land, dismisses the dialog, and does it again. With the checks switched off, the agent has no way to notice, and carries on as if nothing happened.

Across 44 runs, with the redesigns and interruptions drawn from a held-out seed, copying the clicks finished the task three times. Eye-doss finished 41, and its own verdict matched the truth every time. When a dialog interrupted the task, Eye-doss finished 14 of 16. With the checks off, zero.

The same idea works off the screen. From a demonstration video of blocks being stacked, Eye-doss learns the order, and each placement becomes a physical contract: green on blue, then yellow on green. A simulated robot arm runs the skill and checks every placement through its own cameras. When the table gets bumped and the stack falls, Eye-doss notices and rebuilds it. With the checks off, the robot reports success next to a fallen stack.

Eye-doss is designed around Meta's models. In the design, SAM 3.1 tracks the pointer and segments what changed. Muse Spark reads each step. Muse Wonder compiles the program. And Muse Image draws each skill's card. Everything you just saw ran offline, with classic vision standing in for each model, so every result can be reproduced.
Prompting is how we talk to AI. Showing is how we'll teach it. This is Eye-doss.
